heading: Which compiler each language uses
body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart, C++, Ruby, Lua or Python reaches the browser as WebAssembly. A release build (`ty bundle`) compiles each of these languages with the compiler and settings that make the smallest download. `ty preview` keeps fast settings, so a change shows up in about a second. After a release build, `ty bundle` prints one line for each language: which compiler it used and why (ADR 0081; an ADR is an architecture decision record).

| Language | Release build | Why this compiler | Development build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | rustc with `opt-level=z`, LTO and one codegen unit, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | rustc already makes small modules; these settings and `wasm-opt` remove what is left | rustc with `opt-level=s` |
| Swift | swiftc with `-Osize` and the static standard library, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | swiftc makes a module without Foundation; `wasm-opt` removes what is left | swiftc with `-Osize`, no Binaryen |
| Go | TinyGo with `-opt=z` and the Boehm garbage collector, then `wasm-opt -Oz` | TinyGo leaves out most of the Go runtime, so the module is many times smaller | the standard Go compiler |
| C# and F# | the trimmed .NET interpreter, with Emscripten `-Oz` | the interpreter is the smallest .NET download and fast enough for state and logic | no native relink |
| Kotlin | the Kotlin/Wasm production build, with Binaryen | Kotlin's own production step makes the program about three times smaller | no Binaryen |
| Java | javac, TeaVM's WasmGC backend, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | TeaVM keeps only the Java classes the service uses; `wasm-opt` makes the module about half as large. Tachyon changes TeaVM's `runtime.js` so that it makes no code from text, which Tachyon's content security policy forbids, and gives the behavior runtime simple text checks instead of TeaVM's regular expressions | TeaVM, no Binaryen |
| Dart | `dart compile wasm -O4` | `-O4` also drops runtime type checks, so the module is smaller and faster | `-O2`, with the type checks |
| Ruby | the pinned mruby runtime, built with Emscripten | one runtime for every Ruby service, built once on your machine | the same |
| Lua | the Lua 5.4 runtime, from the pinned lua.org source with Emscripten `-Oz` | one runtime of about 170 KB for every Lua service, built once on your machine | the same |
| C++ | em++ (Emscripten 6.0.10 or newer) with `-Oz`, `-fwasm-exceptions` and emmalloc; `-Oz` also runs Binaryen | Emscripten links only the parts of libc++ that the services use, and Tachyon's JSON prelude avoids `std::to_chars`, so a page with one small service loads about 75 KB (29 KB with Brotli) | em++ with `-O1` |
| Python | the pinned Pyodide 314.0.7 core files, prebuilt and checked by SHA-256, copied from the Tachyon cache | Tachyon never downloads or compiles Python; one runtime of about 13 MB before compression serves every Python service | the same |

Binaryen (its `wasm-opt` program) and TinyGo are optional. Without them a release build still works; the module is larger, and the build line says what to install. `ty doctor` lists both when your project has a Rust, Go, Swift or Java web service. TeaVM itself is not optional: a Java web service needs it in every build, and `ty doctor --install` downloads it into the Tachyon cache. Kotlin needs the kotlin-stdlib-wasm-js 2.1.10 library: set `TAC_KOTLIN_WASM_STDLIB` to its `.klib` file. Swift needs the Swift SDK for WebAssembly: set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_SDK` to its `wasm32-unknown-wasip1` folder, and set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_COMPILER` to the swift.org swiftc when another swiftc, such as Xcode's, comes first on PATH. Python needs its five pinned Pyodide files in `python-web/314.0.7/` in the Tachyon cache, and `ty doctor` checks them.

Ruby, Lua and Python ship a runtime that was not written by Tachyon, so a build that copies one also writes its license notices beside it in `.tachyon/services/`: `ruby/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`, `lua/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` and `python/314.0.7/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`. The Python file holds the licenses of Pyodide (MPL-2.0, with the address of its source code), CPython (PSF License) and the libraries inside `pyodide.asm.wasm`. The Ruby and Lua files also hold the licenses of the parts of Emscripten that the runtime links in: Emscripten itself, musl and compiler-rt. Deploy these files with the app.
